aggregate.def: A function that turns many rows into one value: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN or MAX.

count-column.def: Counts the rows where that column isn't NULL. COUNT(*) counts every row.

group-by.def: Sorts rows into groups that share a value, then returns one row per group. Aggregates are computed per group.

grain.def: What one row of a result stands for: one order, one customer, one day. GROUP BY sets it.

bare-column.def: A selected column that's neither grouped nor aggregated. PostgreSQL rejects it; SQLite quietly picks a value from some row.

having.def: Filters groups after GROUP BY, using aggregates. WHERE filters rows before grouping.

count-distinct.def: Counts different values once each. The usual fix when a join has repeated rows.

lines.hook.1: So far, every query returned rows. Now the bakery wants numbers.
lines.hook.2: How many orders came in? What sells best? Who are the regulars?
lines.hook.3: Each answer squeezes many rows into a few. That's what this lesson is about.
lines.goals.intro: Here's what you'll be able to do by the end of this lesson.
lines.goals.1: One. Turn many rows into one value with COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX, and know which NULLs they skip.
lines.goals.2: Two. Group rows with GROUP BY, say what one result row stands for, and keep every column grouped or aggregated.
lines.goals.3: Three. Filter rows with WHERE and groups with HAVING, and count correctly after a join.
lines.agg.2: COUNT star turns them into one row, with one number: sixteen.
lines.agg.3: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX each turn many rows into one value. They're called <k id="aggregate">aggregate functions</k>.

agg.4.caption: On the eight products: the prices add up to 36.10, and average 4.51. Cheapest 2.80, dearest 6.50.
agg.4.voice: On the eight products: the prices add up to thirty-six ten, and average four fifty-one. The cheapest is two eighty, the dearest six fifty.

lines.count.ask: Ten customers. How many does COUNT of phone return?
lines.count.ten: It's seven. Three customers have no phone.
lines.count.seven: Seven. You remembered the missing phones.
lines.count.three: Three is how many are missing. COUNT of phone returns seven.
lines.count.1: <k id="count-column">COUNT of a column</k> skips NULLs. COUNT star counts every row. Interviewers love that difference.
lines.group.1: Next question: how many orders are paid, pending, or refunded?
lines.group.2: GROUP BY status sorts the rows into one pile per status.
lines.group.3: Then each pile collapses into a single row, and COUNT runs once per pile.
lines.group.4: Three statuses, three rows. That's <k id="group-by">GROUP BY</k>.
lines.group.5: The result has a new <k>grain</k>: one row per status, not one per order. Always know the grain of your result.
lines.city.1: Your turn. How many customers live in each city?
lines.city.ask: Write the query: the city, and a count.

city.hint.caption: SELECT city, COUNT(*) from customers, then GROUP BY city.
city.hint.voice: Select the city and count star from customers, then group by city.

lines.city.error: The database couldn't run that. The message under the editor says why.
lines.city.extra: Too many rows. Is there a GROUP BY?
lines.city.missing: Some cities are missing, or the counts are off. Group by city and count every row.
lines.city.columns: Just two columns: the city, and the count.
lines.city.done: Seven rows. Notice NULL: Raj has no city, and missing values form a group of their own.

bare.1.caption: Here's a mistake that's easy to make. Group orders by customer, but also select ordered_at.
bare.1.voice: Here's a mistake that's easy to make. Group orders by customer, but also select the order date.

lines.bare.2: Maya has four orders, with four dates. Her group gets one row. Which date goes in it?
lines.bare.3: PostgreSQL refuses to guess, and rejects the query. SQLite quietly picks one. That's a <k id="bare-column">bare column</k>.
lines.bare.4: The rule: every selected column is either grouped, or wrapped in an aggregate. MAX of ordered at gives Maya's latest order.
lines.having.1: The bakery wants its regulars: customers with at least two orders.
lines.having.2: WHERE can't do it. It runs before grouping, and there's no count yet.
lines.having.3: <k id="having">HAVING</k> filters groups, after they're counted. Maya, Omar, Ana and Yuki make the cut.
lines.having.4: Now count only paid orders. WHERE drops the unpaid rows first, then the groups are counted.
lines.having.yes: Look again. Omar's second order is still pending.
lines.having.no: Right. One of Omar's two orders is pending.
lines.having.5: WHERE filters rows before grouping. HAVING filters groups after. The full order is FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT.
lines.best.1: Your turn. The bakery wants its best sellers: products that sold at least five units in total.
lines.best.ask: Group by product name, and keep the big groups.

best.hint.caption: Sum the quantity per product, then HAVING SUM(i.quantity) >= 5.
best.hint.voice: Sum the quantity per product, then keep the groups having a sum of at least five.

lines.best.error: The database couldn't run that. Read the message, then try again.
lines.best.extra: Too many products. Filter the groups with HAVING.
lines.best.missing: Some best sellers are missing. Are you summing the quantity, not counting rows?
lines.best.columns: Two columns: the product's name, and its total.
lines.best.done: Four products. Croissants lead with ten.
lines.fanout.1: Last trap, and it's one you've seen before. Count each customer's orders, but also join their items.
lines.fanout.2: Maya shows seven orders. She has four. The join repeated each order once per item.
lines.fanout.3: COUNT star counts rows, and fan-out made extra rows.
lines.fanout.4: <k id="count-distinct">COUNT DISTINCT</k> on the order ID counts each order once. Maya's back to four.
lines.fanout.5: When a joined total looks too big, check the grain before you trust it.
lines.recap.intro: Let's look back at what you can do now.
lines.recap.1: An aggregate squeezes many rows into one value. COUNT star counts rows. COUNT of phone skips the three missing phones: ten versus seven.
lines.recap.2: GROUP BY turns each pile of rows into one row. That's the grain. Every other column needs an aggregate, never a bare column.
lines.recap.3: WHERE drops rows before grouping. HAVING drops groups after they're counted. Count only paid orders, and Omar is no longer a regular.
lines.check.intro: Now three quick checks. Each asks you to use an idea, not just name it.

check.q1.caption: COUNT(city) and COUNT(DISTINCT city) on the customers. Raj has no city; the rest live in six different cities. What comes back?
check.q1.voice: Count of city, and count distinct city, on the customers. Raj has no city, and the rest live in six different cities. What comes back?

lines.check.q1-why: Nine and six. COUNT of city skips Raj's NULL. DISTINCT counts each city once, and NULL is never counted.

check.q2.caption: SELECT category, name, SUM(price) FROM products GROUP BY category. What's wrong?
check.q2.voice: Select the category, the name, and the sum of the prices from products, grouped by category. What's wrong?

lines.check.q2-why: Name is a bare column. Each category has several products, so there's no single name. Postgres rejects it; SQLite quietly picks one.
lines.check.q3: Products with at least five units sold, counting only paid orders. Where does each condition go?
lines.check.q3-why: The status is a fact about one row, so it goes in WHERE, before grouping. The sum only exists per group, so it goes in HAVING.

check.pass.caption: {right} / 3. The ideas are sticking.
check.pass.voice: Nicely done. The ideas are sticking.

check.retry.caption: {right} / 3. The goals marked revisit are the ones to replay.
check.retry.voice: A few to revisit. The goals marked revisit at the end are the ones to replay.

lines.interview.intro: Now an interview round. Two quick questions, then one you answer in your own words.

interview.w1.caption: What's the difference between WHERE and HAVING?
interview.w1.speaker: interviewer

lines.interview.w1-why: WHERE runs before grouping, on single rows, so it can't see a count. HAVING runs after, on whole groups.

interview.w2.caption: When do COUNT(*) and COUNT(column) give different answers?
interview.w2.voice: When do count star and count of a column give different answers?
interview.w2.speaker: interviewer

lines.interview.w2-why: When the column has NULLs. COUNT star counts rows; COUNT of a column counts the values that aren't NULL.

interview.open.caption: Write a query for each customer's number of orders and total spend. Then tell me what could make those numbers wrong.
interview.open.speaker: interviewer

lines.interview.think: Take a minute. Say your answer out loud, as if you were in the room, or jot some notes. Then reveal the model answer.
lines.interview.reveal: Here's what an interviewer listens for. Tick the points you covered.
lines.interview.rate: Be honest. How did you do?
lines.interview.got: Nice. That's an answer that lands.
lines.interview.partly: Good start. It's in your flashcards now, so it'll come back.
lines.interview.missed: That's what practice is for. It's in your flashcards, and it'll come back.

lines.finish.1: That's the lesson. Aggregates squeeze rows into numbers. GROUP BY sets the grain. And HAVING filters the groups.
